prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset: production sprite atlas for Cosmic: A Sea Beneath the Moon. Input image1 is a STYLE reference only: retain the medallion form, palette, grain and physical depiction approach, but create the NEW requested subjects below. Exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, 16 circles total. Regular equal square cells, Use a SQUARE canvas, exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, equal square cells, no outer margin. Aim2048px wide. Every circle diameter84%of its cell, centred, with generous fully transparent gutters; leave allcells complete and separated. No extra cells or objects. Original astronomical chromolithograph with dry-gouache and chalk masses: deep indigo circular fields, feathered warm-ivory light, amber heat, copper/charcoal minerals and restrained teal water. Simplify to broad meaningful structures visible at72px. Fine grain stays in subjects; generous quiet dark space. One thin ivory circular outline. No glossy UI buttons, photographic lens flare, ornamental decoration, humans, machines, text, labels, numerals, formulas or grid lines. Inside each circle the field is opaque; outside circles true alpha transparency. No shadows, rays or fragments beyond circles. Atom/particle diagrams are schematic: tiny compact ivory dots and diffuse electron-probability clouds, never planetary electron orbits; individual nuclei do NOT glow like stars. Exact invisible chemistry is communicated by game names/readings, never by invented diagnostic coloration. All terrestrial worlds have bare mineral terrain; no plants, life or modern continents. Early Moon is pale gray-ivory without familiar dark maria. All Earth cutaways are views of one continuing world.
Strict row-major subjects (left to right, then top to bottom):
1. Water spreading over the beach: Teal water covers most of the established dark sand crescent, leaving only a narrow upper dry margin. Avoid: Same bay geometry at high water; no new beach or storm-breaking wave emphasis.
2. A beach exposed by the falling tide: The same bay exposes a broad wet dark sand crescent with a lower receding teal waterline. Avoid: Wet sheen and widened exposed strip show withdrawal; no added shells, algae or footprints.
3. Seawater filling rock hollows: High teal seawater connects the established twin rock hollows to the surrounding sea over their low outer rims. Avoid: Continuous high-water connection visible; isolated retained pools belong to the next state.
4. Pools left behind by the tide: The same twin hollows hold separated teal pools behind raised basalt rims, the sea visibly lower beyond. Avoid: Dry connecting rock and lower sea show tidal retention; no organisms.
5. Earth’s near and far sides: A bare-rock and teal Earth beside a smaller pale Moon, three unlabelled surface dots aligned along their connecting direction. Avoid: Near/centre/far geometry without force arrows; no familiar continents or straight physical tether.
6. The coastal wind easing: Two fading air strokes taper above a dark sheltered pool and dim teal sea, small ripples dying away. Avoid: Wind easing, not a thermometer, snowfall or moon reflection already present.
7. A rocky rise behind the shore: The established bare basalt ridge rises behind a lower coastal slope, broad simple silhouette under pale moist air. Avoid: Dry ridge geometry before rainfall; no trees, grass or claimed named mountain range.
8. Water evaporating from the sea: A broad teal sea surface beneath warm oblique sunlight sends two faint upward evaporation cues into clear air. Avoid: Vapor itself is invisible; no boiling ocean or solid mineral grains rising with water.
9. A cloud made from seawater: A small pale droplet cloud sits above the established teal sea, generous dark air between cloud and water. Avoid: Sea source context; same ordinary droplet appearance as earlier clouds.
10. A cloud carried over land: The same pale cloud crosses from the sea edge toward the bare basalt ridge on one sparse lateral cue. Avoid: Transport over land, no rainfall yet and no new independent water source.
11. Rain on the rocky rise: The same cloud lifts along the basalt ridge and releases a short curtain of rain onto its bare upper slope. Avoid: Local terrain-forced rainfall; no forest, river already formed or freezing snow.
12. A stream returning to the sea: A narrow clear teal stream follows the familiar basalt slope into the open sea, viewed from above its mouth. Avoid: A complete sea-bound route after rain; freshwater chemistry remains invisible.
13. A still pool at night: One of the established rimmed rock pools holds a smooth dark teal surface with a single dim edge glint. Avoid: No lunar disk reflection yet; calmness distinguished from rippled connected sea.
14. Sunlight reflected by the Moon: The established pale early Moon has a lit ivory crescent and one sparse incoming and outgoing light-ray cue. Avoid: Reflected sunlight, no self-generated amber glow and no dark maria.
15. Moonlight across the sea: The pale early Moon above open teal sea casts a broad broken ivory reflection path across small wavelets; bare coast at edge. Avoid: Wide moving sea with fragmented light, no mirror disk or living shoreline.
16. The Moon reflected in a rock pool: The established single rock pool contains a soft pale lunar disk reflection, tiny ripples break its edge; dark basalt rim surrounds it. Avoid: Small enclosed pool, recognizable calm reflection; no second physical Moon underwater.

Image2 is the APPROVED COAST GEOGRAPHY reference. For any shore or pool subject keep its stepped LEFT headland and low RIGHT ridge. Any hollows/pools are the same threebasins: LARGE foreground-right pool, smaller mid-left pool and small distant middle pool, same connecting basalt rims. Waterlevel orlighting maychange; rockgeometry andcamera mustnot. Water-chemistry detailviews may use closer crops of these materials. No invented bottles, vessels, observers or biological scenery.
